intendedStory: Begin with the accusation and apparently self-incriminating defense; reveal that authenticity was the dangerous allegation; reconstruct why the paintings were believed; follow the problem of proving that accepted masterpieces were modern; end with forensic evidence and fraud conviction, without turning a self-serving defense into heroism.
whySelected: Selected on absolute merit: confession normally worsens a criminal case, but here exposes the central mistaken premise of a more serious accusation. Anticipated answer “it was a fake” opens the stronger questions of how an accepted masterpiece could be fabricated and how the confession could be tested. Unlike a one-fact reversal, resin and missing-period expectations connect deception to evidence.
